titre: The wolves that supposedly changed the course of rivers
accroche: A famous story makes the wolves of Yellowstone the architects of an ecosystem. Ecologists are divided
contenu_vulgarise:
The wolf had disappeared from Yellowstone in the mid-1920s, exterminated. Thirty-one individuals were reintroduced starting in 1995.

The story that circulated afterward became one of the most widely shared texts in popular ecology. Wolves reduce the number of elk and change their habits; elk stop lingering in the valley bottoms; willows and poplars grow back there; beavers return and build dams; the banks stabilize, and rivers change course.

Wolves that change the course of rivers: the image is irresistible, and that is a problem.

## What is solidly established

The general mechanism, the trophic cascade, is real and documented elsewhere. A top predator can alter vegetation by acting on herbivores, through direct predation as well as through the fear it inspires.

At Yellowstone, several observations hold up. The elk population has declined sharply. Browsing of young shoots has dropped markedly, from nearly all the stems measured in the late 1990s to under a quarter a decade later, on the tallest stems in each plot, as the authors themselves specify, an indicator of the leading edge of recruitment rather than a random sample of the whole stand. An independent random sample finds a much smaller decline, the initial method having overestimated the recovery by a factor of 4 to 7; and aspen cover continues to decline at the landscape scale, from about 4% in the early 20th century to 1% in the mid-1990s and then 0.25% in 2021. Studies have shown elk staying more at forest edges, where they can see danger coming.

## What is much less so

The full sequence, however, is disputed by part of the community, including some of the most respected wolf specialists.

The objections concern attribution. The decline in elk is not explained by wolves alone: hunting, several harsh winters, a prolonged drought, and the return of bears and cougars all played a part at the same time. The recovery of willows is real in places, absent elsewhere, and seems to depend as much on available water as on browsing pressure.

As for the rivers, the effect is the furthest along the causal chain, and therefore the most fragile: every link would have to have held, over a period in which many other factors shifted.

The debate is not closed. A reassessment published in 2025 puts the effect on willows among the strongest ever measured for this type of cascade; a commentary published in the same journal disputes this calculation, judging the model circular and the compared plots unmatched, and concludes, from the same data, a modest effect that varies by location rather than a strong, widespread cascade.

## Why that story won

It has everything that makes a story circulate: a culprit exterminated by mistake, a return, a repair, and a conclusion visible from a helicopter.

The cautious version says the same thing less sharply: a real effect, of debated magnitude, mixed in with other causes, varying from valley to valley. It doesn't get shared.

There is a difficulty here that ecology runs into more than other disciplines. Its objects are systems where everything acts on everything, and where isolating a cause takes decades. The one-link story is false by construction, and yet it is the only format that travels.

repere.texte: Among the five tallest stems in each plot, an indicator of the “leading edge” of recruitment, as the authors specify, not a random sample, browsing of young aspen shoots went from all of the stems measured in 1998 to under a quarter in dry areas and under a fifth along streams in 2010.
repere.source: Ripple & Beschta, “Trophic cascades in Yellowstone: The first 15 years after wolf reintroduction,” Biological Conservation, 145, 2012

carte.punch: The one-link story is false by construction. It is the only one that travels.
carte.idee: The wolves reintroduced to Yellowstone supposedly made willows grow back and changed the course of rivers. The effect on browsing is real; its magnitude and the share of other causes, hunting, drought, other predators, remain debated.

quiz.question: What makes the “wolves change rivers” link the most fragile?
choix: No decline in elk numbers was measured after the reintroduction
The trophic cascade mechanism is not documented anywhere else
It is the furthest link in the chain, and therefore the most exposed to other causes
The reintroduced wolves were too few to have a measurable effect
quiz.explication: The decline in elk and the decline in browsing are documented, and trophic cascades are an established mechanism. But each additional link multiplies the competing explanations, hunting, drought, other predators, available water, and the course of rivers is the most distant of all.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, how many wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone starting in 1995?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that thirty-one individuals were reintroduced starting in 1995, after the wolf's local extermination in the mid-1920s.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, by what means can a top predator alter vegetation in a trophic cascade?
choix: Through direct predation and through the fear it inspires in herbivores
Only by browsing the young shoots itself
By altering the chemical composition of forest soils
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text indicates that the mechanism acts on herbivores as much through direct predation as through the fear the predator inspires in them, which changes their habits.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does an independent random sample of browsing show, compared with the method of the five tallest stems in each plot?
choix: A strictly identical decline, confirming the initial method without reservation
An increase in browsing rather than a decline, across the whole park
An even sharper decline than the one measured by the initial method
A much smaller decline, the initial method having overestimated the recovery by a factor of 4 to 7
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that an independent random sample finds a much smaller decline in browsing, the initial method based on the tallest stems having overestimated the recovery by a factor of 4 to 7.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the commentary published in the same journal as the 2025 reassessment conclude, from the same data?
choix: A full confirmation of the 1,500% increase in willow volume
A modest effect that varies by location, rather than a strong, widespread cascade
A complete absence of any effect of wolves on the park's vegetation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The commentary judges the model circular and the plots unmatched, and concludes a modest effect that varies by location rather than a strong, widespread cascade.
